In Kristjánsson, Jóhannesson & Thornton (2014, *PLoS ONE*), people
foraged for two types of target on a touch screen, in two conditions:
**feature** foraging, where targets differ from distractors in colour
alone, and **conjunction** foraging, where they differ in a combination of
colour and shape. A well-known result is that in conjunction foraging
people tend to collect one target type before switching to the other
(long runs), but switch freely in feature foraging.

This page shows how to work with a fitted model: checking convergence,
reading the posterior, accuracy and posterior predictive checks. It ends with a model comparison: the full transition matrix against a symmetric one.
The model is the default one: multi-level, Fourier-124 directions, the
default priors, 4 chains of 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations.

*Note*: this page doesn't fit anything. It reads saved fits
(`kristjansson2014_fourier124.rds` and `kristjansson2014_fourier124_symmetric.rds`) from `fits/` in this folder.
They aren't in the repository: to make them, run `fit_kristjansson2014plos.R` in this
folder (about 2.5 hours on a laptop), which saves them there. See
`examples/real_data/README.md`.

*Note*: the importer rotates this dataset by 180 degrees, so that first
selections start top-left as in the other datasets. That orientation is an
assumption, so read the absolute-direction results with care.

Code: `kristjansson2014plos.R`.

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::read_chunk("kristjansson2014plos.R")
```

## Accuracy

The fit doesn't store a prediction for every selection
(`save_selections = FALSE`, the default), so `predict_fomo()` makes them
from 200 posterior draws. Deterministic accuracy is how often the item the
model judges most likely is the one selected; the probability of the
chosen item credits being nearly right too. Chance (dotted) is
1 / items left; the nearest-neighbour rule (dashed) always picks the
closest item, so the gap above it is what the model adds to proximity
alone. This is in-sample accuracy, which overestimates out-of-sample
accuracy.

```{r predict}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/kristjansson2014_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d))
```

```{r fig-accuracy}
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy at each selection, with chance and nearest-neighbour baselines."
```

## Posterior predictive check

Whole trials simulated from the fitted model, compared with the data. The
model doesn't predict when a trial stops, so each simulated trial keeps as
many selections as the observed one.

```{r sim-posterior}

#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/kristjansson2014_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d), n_post_draws)
```

## Model comparison: Symmetric transition matrix?

The model above gives each condition a full 2 x 2 transition matrix: the
probability of staying with a target type can differ between the two
types, so one type can be preferred overall. A simpler model has one
parameter per condition, the probability of staying with the type just
selected, the same for both types (`prep_stan_list(symmetric_v = TRUE)`,
`cat_sym.stan`): the matrix is symmetric and neither type is preferred.
Everything else is the same, and so are the fit's settings. The
comparison asks whether the asymmetry earns its extra parameters.

```{r compare-load}
```

`fomo_compare()` tabulates accuracy (against the nearest-neighbour rule)
and loo: `elpd_diff` is the difference from the best model, `se_diff` its
standard error, and `robust` whether the difference survives dropping the
trials with unreliable (high Pareto k) loo estimates.

```{r compare}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/kristjansson2014_fourier124.rds"), file.mtime("fits/kristjansson2014_fourier124_symmetric.rds"), rlang::hash(d))
```

The full matrix is clearly better: about 241 elpd ahead (SE 44), with few
trials of unreliable loo (about 1%), so the difference is robust. The plot
below shows where it comes from. In **feature** search the symmetric model
does as well, slightly better even (8 ± 5 elpd, within 2 SE): people stay
with the type just selected about two-thirds of the time (stay log-odds
0.72, a probability of about 0.67), and the two types are treated alike.
All of the full model's advantage is in **conjunction** search (250 ± 43):
there people almost always stay with the type just selected, but more so
for one type than the other: in the full model the stay log-odds are
about 4.9 for type 1 and 2.9 for type 2 (probabilities about 0.99 and
0.95; in feature search 0.73 and 0.71, alike). Leaving one type is rarer
than leaving the other, which one stay probability for both can't
capture. So the asymmetry is needed,
but only for conjunction foraging.

```{r fig-compare}
#| fig-cap: "Difference in loo between the full and symmetric models, summed over each condition's trials (point: sum; bars: 2 SE)."
```
